ns0:entry.ns0:title: [Apple Explained]How A Single Ad Campaign Saved The Mac

ns2:group.ns2:title: How A Single Ad Campaign Saved The Mac
ns2:group.ns2:description:
Get Tidy Today! Try CleanMyMac 7 days FREE and use my code APPLEEXPLAINED for 20% off - https://clnmy.com/AppleExplained20
______
Apple has had some pretty iconic commercials. Ridley Scott’s ‘1984’ Super Bowl ad introduced the Macintosh as a challenge to IBM’s dominance. The computer it promoted helped bring a mouse and graphical interface to a much wider audience, building on work Apple had already done with the Lisa. The iPod silhouette campaign, which began in 2003, served a different purpose. Darkened dancers against bright backgrounds made the white iPod and its headphone cables instantly visible. The ads presented portable music as something expressive and desirable, just as Apple was expanding beyond Mac owners.

ns2:group.ns2:description:
Thanks to @FitnexaAI for sponsoring this video. Check out Fitnexa SomniPods 3 here and get $10 off: https://go.fitnexa.com/3kOvyG Coupon code: AppleExplained #Fitnexa #SomniPods3 #SleepEarbuds #sleeptechnology
Do your AirPods fall out while sleeping? Check out SomniPods 3 from Fitnexa; the earbuds that stay secure all night. ________
The headphones that came with the original iPod couldn’t adjust the volume. There was no button or slider anywhere on the cable. If you wanted it louder, you had to pull the iPod out of your pocket and spin a scroll wheel. There was no microphone either. But that mattered less in 2001, since the iPod couldn’t make calls. And there was definitely no active noise cancellation, so the only thing standing between you and the sound of traffic was a black foam covering that Apple included in the box.
Today, Apple sells headphones that measure your heart rate, translate a conversation in real time, and function as a hearing aid. The evolution between those two products is one of the most interesting in Apple's history, because for the first fifteen years of it, Apple's headphone business didn’t appear in a single financial document. While today, it’s a category that out-earns entire most fortune 500 companies.

ns0:entry.ns0:title: [Apple Explained]Why Apple Removed The Glowing Logo From MacBooks

ns2:group.ns2:title: Why Apple Removed The Glowing Logo From MacBooks
ns2:group.ns2:description: The glowing Apple logo on the back of a MacBook was never a light. There was no bulb behind it, no dedicated LED, no wire running to it, and no way to turn it off manually. That’s because it was just a hole in the display enclosure. Apple cut a logo-shaped opening straight through the aluminum lid, capped it with a piece of translucent plastic, and let the screen's own backlight spill out the back. So when people say Apple removed the glowing logo, that isn't quite what happened. Apple filled in a hole it could no longer leave open. And the reasons come down to engineering issues, durability issues, and a new design direction.

ns2:group.ns2:description:

For almost twenty years, Apple sold a computer called the Mac Pro. It was their most powerful and pricey desktop made for professionals. This past March, Apple stopped making it. With the model disappearing from Apple's website, and the company confirming to tech outlet 9to5Mac that it had no plans to build another.
For most people, this news was irrelevant. The Mac Pro never sold in very high volume since it was made for a small market of power users that could afford to spend six-thousand-dollars or more on their machine.
In this video I’ll explain the biggest factors that contributed to Apple ending the Mac Pro line, and what that means for people who used them.
